prompt.context: Two of your business school classmates, despite trends indicating otherwise, opened a video rental store near the HBS campus. Their first two years saw unprecedented success — they bought matching Porsches and a townhouse in Beacon Hill. However, about 12 months later, after two and a half years of dramatic profit and revenue growth, profits have dramatically fallen. They come to you for help, saying: 'We don't know what happened and our mortgage and car payments are getting tougher to meet.'
prompt.question: What do you think the problem is? Diagnose the situation and identify the root cause of the profit decline.

clarifying_info.a: Revenues have decreased; cost is probably not the primary problem.
No, the price of video rentals has not changed.

clarifying_info.q: Are fewer customers coming to the store, or is each customer renting fewer videos?
clarifying_info.a: Traffic (number of customers coming to the store) has fallen.

clarifying_info.q: Has a new video store opened in the area?
Has a new movie theatre opened in the area?
Have there been other competitive or macro changes?
clarifying_info.a: Probe further — think carefully about how you define the client's business and competitive set.

framework: 1. Diagnose the P&L: determine whether the profit decline is driven by revenue decline or cost increase
2. Decompose revenue: Revenue = Number of videos rented × Price per rental
3. Identify whether the revenue issue is a traffic problem (fewer customers entering) or a share-of-wallet problem (existing customers renting fewer videos)
4. For traffic decline: assess macro factors vs. competitive factors
5. Define the client's business correctly: not just 'video rental' but 'home movie entertainment' — broadening the competitive set
6. Identify the true competitor: home delivery, cable, pay-per-view, or Video-on-Demand technologies eating into store traffic

questions.prompt: If profits have declined, is it driven by revenue decline or cost increase? Why is cost probably not the main issue here?
questions.guidance: Video rental is a high fixed-cost business — rent, inventory (videos), and labor are largely fixed relative to rental revenue. Therefore profit is highly sensitive to changes in revenue (capacity utilization), not cost. The student should identify this quickly and focus on revenue.

questions.prompt: Revenue = price × quantity. Prices have not changed. So is the problem fewer customers visiting, or each customer renting fewer videos on average?
questions.guidance: Student should propose a data-driven diagnostic: use the store's security counter to measure traffic year-over-year, and use register receipts to compute videos rented per customer per visit. Comparing this year vs. last year reveals whether it is a traffic problem or a share-of-wallet problem.

questions.prompt: If it were a share-of-wallet problem, what would you think is causing it?
questions.guidance: Share-of-wallet problems are typically driven by internal execution issues: poor selection, bad customer service, unfavorable store layout, etc. Traffic problems are more often externally driven — market or competitive factors.

questions.prompt: Data shows traffic has fallen. No new video store and no new movie theatre have opened. What hypotheses can you generate for why traffic is down?
questions.guidance: The student should now recognize that the competitive set is not just other video rental stores. The client is in the 'home movie entertainment' business. Competitors include: home delivery (mail/DVD-by-mail services), cable TV, pay-per-view (PPV), and emerging Video-on-Demand / Movie-on-Demand technology. One of these substitute services has likely infiltrated or grown rapidly in the market, reducing the addressable pool of customers for in-store rental.

brainstorming.prompt: How would you define your client's competitive set, and what alternative entertainment options might be drawing customers away from the video store?

categories.name: In-store video rental substitutes
ideas: Larger chain (e.g., Blockbuster) entering the area

categories.name: Home delivery / mail rental
ideas: DVD-by-mail services (e.g., Netflix) offering convenience without a trip to the store

categories.name: Cable and broadcast television
ideas: Pay-per-view (PPV) movies available without leaving home

categories.name: Digital / on-demand
ideas: Video-on-Demand (VOD) or Movie-on-Demand services through cable operators
Early streaming or download-to-own digital services

categories.name: Other home entertainment
ideas: Increased internet usage and online entertainment

categories.name: Macro / lifestyle factors
ideas: Demographic shifts in the neighborhood (fewer movie renters)

recommendation: The primary driver of profit decline is a traffic decline — fewer customers are visiting the store, not a price or internal execution issue.

The root cause is almost certainly a competitive disruption from within the broader 'home movie entertainment' category — likely the growth of home delivery services, cable/PPV, or early Video-on-Demand technology — which has reduced the total pool of customers willing to make a trip to a physical rental store.
risks: If the shift to on-demand / delivery entertainment is structural and accelerating, in-store rental revenue will continue to decline regardless of operational improvements.
Attempting to compete on price alone may be insufficient if customers value convenience over cost.
next_steps: Confirm which specific substitute(s) have grown in the area (survey customers, check cable/VOD adoption rates in the neighborhood).
Evaluate whether the business can pivot — e.g., add a delivery/reservation service, partner with digital platforms, or diversify product offerings.
Assess financial runway: can the current fixed-cost structure survive while a turnaround is attempted?
